narrative:
The model determined that you have a 91.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants to admit students likely to succeed, this strong prediction of failure led to the rejection of your application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your class ranking after the first year of law school, your class ranking after the third year, and your LSAT score. Your first-year and third-year rankings were by far the strongest drivers, and both pushed the prediction sharply toward failure. While most admitted students ranked around the middle of their class (average around the 6th decile), you placed in the bottom decile in both periods. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 37 was almost identical to the average of accepted students (37.18). This actually worked slightly in your favor and pulled the prediction a little toward passing, but it was not nearly enough to offset the impact of your class rankings.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA of 3.10 (versus 3.23 for accepted students), gender, race, and full-time status played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in law school if possible, or consider retaking the LSAT for a substantially higher score. Strengthening these key areas will be the most effective way to demonstrate readiness for the bar exam in any future applications. (248 words)
